translations.text: The Life-giver’s ascent once crowned us with fitting and festive crowns, for he raised our human nature and planted it in heaven. This was the very beginning of the discourse: that the Savior won every benefit for us. He bestowed nothing upon himself, but gave us salvation, for he made our earthen nature heavenly and established this earth, destined to feed the grave, as a participant in the nature of heaven. For the divine apostle knows how to speak of an image made of dust and a heavenly image. We hear it in his own words: “The first man,” he says, “was from the earth, made of dust; the second man is the Lord from heaven.” And he adds to this: “As is the man made of dust, so also are those made of dust; and as is the heavenly one, so also are the heavenly.” He calls the man “made of dust” not because he came from the earth, but because he performs earthly deeds. And he calls the other “heavenly” not because he received his body from heaven—for he took his body from the Virgin and from the earth—but because he possesses virtue in himself and because his body belongs to the heavenly one. He did not call the body heavenly by nature, but because of the heavenly one who clothed himself in it.

The first man came from dust and conducted himself in earthly deeds. The dust that rises is called dust, while that which bears fruit is called earth. Thus he does not merely call the man earthly, but made of dust, having come into the dust of sins. Just as clothes and eyes are harmed by dust, so souls are harmed by sins. Just as clothes and faces become clean when the dust is shaken off, so, when you cast away your sins, souls become clean and light. As blessed David also says: “Like arrows in the hand of a mighty man, so are the sons of those who have shaken themselves free.” And as he says to Jerusalem: “Rise and shake your dust off yourself.” The heavens likewise take their form according to the man made of dust who is clothed in earthly deeds. When people are smeared with sins as with dust, the heavens also sift down dust. Nor is it strange to say that dust is sifted down from heaven: it comes not from the nature of heaven, but from what those [?] deserve. And who will bear witness to these words? God, through Moses, who said: “If you do not listen to the laws of the Lord your God, your rain shall become dust for you, and dust shall descend from heaven. If you do not abide by the laws of the Lord your God, your rain shall become dust, and dust shall descend from heaven.” Dust is sifted down upon the man made of dust because he has clothed himself in the dust of sins.

Just as he brings forward this example concerning such people—that the heavens will rain dust upon the man made of dust—so he provides what is fitting according to each person’s will. If he sees a hardened mind, he acts according to its hardness; and if a gentle one, according to its gentleness. Indeed, many are hard and unyielding like iron and bronze. As Isaiah also says of Israel: “I knew that you are hard, that your neck is an iron sinew and your forehead bronze.” By “iron sinew” he means the disobedient neck that is irked and avoids coming under the yoke of the worship of God, recoiling from the laws, in accordance with the saying: “Ephraim became a heifer that throws off the yoke, and did not accept the yoke.” When people remain in such hardness, disobedience, and unwillingness to listen, God also changes his creation accordingly: “If you do not listen to my laws, I will make the heavens above you bronze and the earth beneath you iron.” This means that he makes it without seed and without fruit.

In accordance with the earthly person, created things likewise adapt themselves to exact punishment for their evil deeds and their contempt for the Creator’s laws. But for whoever bears the likeness of the heavenly one, in accordance with the saying, “As we have put on the image of the heavenly one,” the heavens likewise adapt themselves; and for whoever has a tender mind, a rain of sweetness pours down. Because he has fulfilled the divine commandments, God fills his fields with heavenly dew. “Receive,” he says, “the dew of my commandments, and I will bring you the dew of rain.” If our souls are watered by the divine commandments, he also waters our fields with beneficial rains. “If you listen to the laws [?], the heavens will give their dew, and the earth its fruit.” The earth bears fruit for the obedient.

From now on, put on the image of the heavenly one. He calls the Savior heavenly not only because he is from heaven—for it is plainly evident that God the Word is not only heavenly but also Lord of heaven and of the angels—but also with respect to the flesh, because on earth he practiced the virtue of heaven. For if he calls the Savior heavenly only because he is from heaven, how does he also call others heavenly, when their nature did not come from heaven? Likewise, blessed David calls him heavenly, for I find that name used once in the Old Testament as well as in the New. Paul says, “Put on the image of the heavenly one,” and David says, “When the heavenly one separates the kings upon it.” Upon it—upon what? Upon the earth.

To learn that David applied the word “heavenly” to the Savior, and that this is not a forced interpretation of the words or merely a shared name, but an agreement attested by the truth of the deeds, learn from the sequence itself that David calls the Savior heavenly. “When the heavenly one makes a separation upon it,” he says, “it will snow on Zalmon: the mountain of God, the rich mountain, the lofty mountain, the rich mountain.” I will state the sequence point by point, so that this may not seem a forced interpretation of contrived words, since we also apply the name “heavenly” to the Savior. Rather, let the sequence and the words of us who are speaking proceed clearly and without any muddled confusion; and let no one consider this a forced interpretation, but a true correspondence. “When the heavenly one separates the kings upon it,” he says, “they will become snow.” And what does it mean for the heavenly one to separate the kings upon the earth?

Here he calls the saints “kings of the earth”—not those who possess worldly honor, but those enlightened by heavenly understanding. Of them Paul says, “If we suffer, we shall also reign with him.” Paul speaks of the kingdom of the saints, not with empty, grandiose words or an abundance of praise that makes his hearers proud. For one can often exaggerate, battering the ears of one’s hearers with grandiose words in order to stir them and draw them toward the matters set before them. But Paul does not deceive by battering them with grandiose words. Indeed, he cannot even speak in a manner worthy of the promises. He himself testifies: “What no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and has not entered the human heart, God has prepared for those who love him.” A kingdom will be given to the saints—not an earthly kingdom, but the heavenly one, like that which the Life-giver possesses. When Pilate asked him, “Are you the king of the Jews?” he said, “My kingdom is not of this world. If it were of this world, my servants would fight for me.” A kingdom will be given to the saints, as Paul says, and Daniel agrees with him. “After this,” he says, “God will establish a great and mighty kingdom that will stand and remain forever.” And again: “The saints of the Most High will receive the kingdom.” And here he says, “When the heavenly one distributes kings over it.”

What does “distributes” mean? To distinguish, to separate. How will he distinguish the kings? It means precisely this: having commanded Paul to be a herald of the kingdom, he sent him to proclaim the kingdom from Jerusalem as far as the regions of Illyricum. He sent one to India, another to the eastern regions, another to the western regions, another to the south, and others to the north. In distributing—that is, in distinguishing and separating—he determined which people ought to obey whom, and who would listen to whom and believe. Accordingly, he sent the heralds as was appropriate for each. “When the heavenly one distributes kings over it,” he says, “they will become snow-white in Zalmon,” that is, they will become white. For the preaching of the apostles made the world white and showed the earth to be whiter than snow. It washed it with the word of truth and wiped it clean, according to the saying, “You will wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.” Pay attention to the sequence: “When the heavenly one distributes kings over it, they will become snow-white in Zalmon.” Zalmon is Hebrew and is translated as “peace” [?], instead of saying, “They will be purified in peace.” Having called the Life-giver heavenly, he then indicates his dispensation in the flesh by calling him a mountain: “The mountain of God, a rich mountain.” He changed the designation “heavenly” to the designation “mountain,” not because he himself changed in his true nature, but because he applies these names to himself in accordance with his dispensation. Our Life-giver is called God, Lord, Creator, Almighty, heavenly, king, and mountain. Concerning this mountain, the blessed prophet Isaiah says: “In the last days,” says the Lord, “the mountain of the Lord and the house of God will be manifest above the tops of the mountains. Many nations will come and say, ‘Come, let us go to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.’ For laws will go out from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, and he will judge among many nations.”

The blessed Daniel also glorifies this mountain beforehand, when he explains the composite image made from various materials, which stood fashioned from gold, silver, bronze, iron, and clay. At the end he says that a stone was cut out without hands, struck the image and crushed it, and the stone became a great mountain [?] and filled the whole world. See how certain statements, however minutely they may be explained, do not agree with spiritual interpretations. For if he were speaking of a visible mountain when he said that the stone became a great mountain and filled the world, the act of filling indicates some benefit; but when a mountain extends over everything, it does not fill but covers. It is clear that he calls the saving work of the Savior a mountain, because it is higher than all beneficial means, higher than the excellence of the Law and the prophets, and higher than the speakers of divine words who wrote the praises. He says, ‘It shall be raised above all the hills.’ And here the Savior himself, speaking about the Church, says to the apostles, ‘A city standing on a mountain cannot be hidden.’ What city? The Church: ‘Jerusalem, built as a city.’ The prophet also calls it a house upon the tops of the mountains. What house? The Church. But take care, lest we say something altogether different and force the truth. Let us also examine testimony appropriate to this, showing that the Church is indeed called a house. Listen to Paul writing to Timothy: ‘So that you may know how you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God.’ And if the Church is the house of the living God, then the prophet rightly said that the house of God is above the tops of the mountains. This means that the Church is above every height. ‘And many nations shall go to the house,’ for many nations do not go to the Jewish [?], but to the Church. And they shall say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob.’ We have said many times who the God of Jacob is according to the meaning of the passage, for the God of Jacob appeared as God and man.

And now the blessed David says, “When the heavenly one scatters kings upon it, snow will fall on Zalmon. A mountain of God, a rich mountain.” He calls the Life-giver’s work of salvation a rich mountain, meaning that it is fertile, strong, and covered with every kind of flower. For richness indicates the ability to bring forth every flower, as he also says elsewhere, “The beauty of the wilderness will grow rich,” and again, “These are the sons of richness.” He calls it a curdled mountain: it gathers and makes firm what is scattered, fluid, and watery. Just as rennet gathers and thickens the liquid substance of milk, bringing what is soft and dispersed into a single union, so afterward it is impossible to separate it from that with which it was united—neither this from that, nor that from this. Likewise, once Christ has united himself with our souls, like rennet with milk, he is not separated or dissolved. Paul’s soul was also like this. Once it was fluid like milk, but after it was united with Christ, he said, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?”

“A mountain of God, a rich mountain, a curdled mountain.” He calls the Life-giver a rich mountain, just as the Scriptures also call the prophets mountains. “His foundations,” he says, “are in the holy mountains.” And elsewhere he likewise says, “You shine wonderfully from the everlasting mountains.” He calls the prophets everlasting mountains, in accordance with the saying, “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, for he has visited his people and brought them salvation, as he spoke through the mouths of his prophets who were from of old.” And for this reason, “You shine wonderfully from the everlasting mountains.” “His foundations”—whose? The Life-giver’s—“are in the holy mountains,” because the foundations of this gospel preaching are the prophetic writings. For this very reason, the apostle makes the statement still clearer, saying, “You are the temple of the living God, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, whose cornerstone is Jesus Christ.”

The prophets are called mountains because, just as a mountain comes from the earth and rises above the earth in height—it is from the earth, yet above it—so the prophets were from among human beings, yet above human beings, and therefore were called mountains. The Life-giver is also called a mountain, because he is related to them according to the flesh, yet in his divinity surpasses all flesh and every human mind. And because the prophets were called mountains and the Life-giver a mountain, people supposed that he was one of the prophets. As he himself says, “Who do people say that I, the Son of Man, am?” And they say, “Some say John the Baptist, some Jeremiah, some Elijah, and some one of the prophets.” They thought that the holy mountain was one of the prophets.

The blessed David says beforehand, “Why do you consider the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell to be among the curdled mountains?” “Who do people say the Son of Man is?” They answered and said, “Some say Jeremiah, some Elijah, and some John the Baptist.” Do you see how the prophet speaks beforehand of their suppositions? “Why,” he says, “do you consider the mountain in which God was pleased to dwell to be among the curdled mountains?” And how did he dwell there? For he did not dwell in the prophets as he did here, as he also says here, “The Lord will dwell in it forever.” There he stayed as a guest for a time, but here he made an everlasting dwelling.

And pay attention to the sequence: how Scripture presents the same one as heavenly, the same one as a mountain, the same one as God, and the same one as the Savior of the universe—the same one, the one who appeared in the world. For it says, “The Lord will dwell there forever,” and then, “God’s chariots are in their tens of thousands.” First it called him heavenly, then a mountain, and then God: “God’s chariots are in their tens of thousands, thousands of guides, and the Lord is among them at Sinai, in the holy place. He ascended on high; he took captivity captive.” The prophet speaks of him whose chariots are in their tens of thousands, with thousands of guides: “He ascended on high; he took captivity captive and gave gifts to the sons of men.” And Paul, taking this and confirming [?] the prophet’s intention, brings it into the meaning of the gospel: “Grace has been given to each one according to the measure of Christ’s gifts.” He also adds the prophet’s testimony to this, for he expressly says, “He ascended on high.” Who is the God who ascended, whose chariots are in their tens of thousands, with a thousand guides? Who could the one who ascended be? It is the one of whom he said, “When the heavenly one scattered kings over them.” For he says, “He ascended on high and took captivity captive.” He sets out the statement and explains it himself: “What does ‘he ascended’ mean, except that he first descended into the lower parts of the earth? The one who descended is also the one who ascended above the heavens.” The prophet says that he gave gifts to people, and the apostle explains who gave the gifts: “The one who ascended above the heavens,” he says, “he gave them.” Just as it says there that he gave, so it also says here: “Some as apostles, some as prophets, some as evangelists.” See the abundance of his divinity! See the glorious one’s authority in glory! “He gave,” it says. He did not ask, but gave.

“He ascended on high and took captivity captive.” What captivity was there on high? Here he calls the cross “on high,” in accordance with the saying, “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up.” It is therefore clear that “on high” refers to the cross, for on the cross he drew to himself all humanity, whom Satan held in exile as captives. For this reason he calls the cross “on high,” because on the cross he broke the tyranny of the tyrants and brought back the captives, in accordance with the saying, “You shall call the captives to release.” Christ took those same captives captive. Satan took them captive in one way, and Christ in another: Satan took them from freedom into slavery, but Christ from slavery into freedom, from unbelief into belief. And because custom had already taken hold, and the very name of captivity was frightening, the world thought that it would be taken captive through the violence of some tyrant. Since it did not know the truth, it prepared to fight against the gospel. But the Giver of Life, concealing the purpose of his love for humanity and advancing in battle array, sends flashes of lightning against his enemies. He showers arrows from the bow of the Spirit, in accordance with what the apostle says: “The weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful for tearing down fortified reasonings and every proud thing raised against the knowledge of Christ; and we take every thought captive into obedience to Christ.” And because his love for humanity [?] captivity, the world thought that “he ascended on high”—onto the cross—“and took captivity captive and gave gifts to people.” When people take captives, they seize their possessions. But the great King’s taking of captives, drawing upon the stream of his love for humanity, took nothing from the captives, but even gave to them.

Such was Paul. He once took others captive while he was deceived by [?], and afterward he himself was taken captive by the power of Christ. And he acknowledged this good captivity: “Mark, my beautiful one, sends you greetings,” he says. He turned from bitter captivity and entered holy captivity. And the Life-giver led him about in the bonds of the gospel as a display and an example—not to disgrace him, but to glorify him. And he considered this captivity so pleasant that he even boasted of the bonds of his captivity. Listen to him: “I appeal to you, I, Paul, an old man, and now also a prisoner of Jesus Christ.” And elsewhere, with chains upon him, he said, “For the hope of Israel I wear these chains.” And he writes to Timothy, “Share in suffering for the gospel, for which I too suffer in bonds like a criminal.” But see the boldness of this chosen soul: “Yet the word of God,” he says, “is not bound. I endure everything for the sake of the elect, so that they may become imitators of me.”

Do you see what captivity he took captive? “He ascended on high,” it says, “and took captivity captive.” From whom? From Satan. For human bodies were vessels of Satan, and vessels of various kinds. Just as in a house one vessel is for oil, another for wine, another for vinegar, and another vessel is made of iron or some other material, and all belong to one house, so Satan took humanity and made vessels of various kinds: some vessels of fornication, some of adultery, some of deceit, some of tyranny, some of greed, some of godlessness, some of blasphemy, some of confused speech, and some of dishonor. The Life-giver came and saw that everyone had been seized. He says to the disciples, “No one can enter the strong man’s house and seize his [?] unless he first binds the strong man, and then seizes his vessels.” He calls Satan strong—not because he was at all strong against him, but against the people who waged war with him. Do you see that the Life-giver too seized those who had been seized and took captive those who had been taken captive?

And indeed, he did what he said. For nowhere do you find that the Giver of Life set his hand to teaching people, set out the details of the word of truth, or led anyone onto the paths of salvation without first binding the devil. When he who sanctifies everyone accepted life-giving baptism, he mixed the good leaven—his own holiness—with the water and placed himself beneath the water, so that he might conceal the power of the leaven beneath it. He was baptized, and immediately [?] went from the Jordan into the wilderness to be tempted by Satan. Pay close attention to this, I beg you: how it agrees with the saying that no one can seize the strong man's possessions unless he first binds the strong man. The Savior is nowhere seen teaching or performing any signs before he first bound Satan in the wilderness, and with him all his wickedness. Then, returning from the wilderness, he begins proclaiming the divine message and takes back those who had been seized by Satan, not through his divine power, but through his work in the flesh. For this was precisely the task before him: to defeat Satan through the flesh, and not through his divinity. For if God were to enter combat with Satan, that would be a disgraceful battle and victory. Rather, as I have said many times, because the enemy's struggle was against human beings, he arms human nature in himself against the adversary, so that it might wound the very one who had wounded it.

And now, having taken from him the vessels—that is, the souls of people who wandered astray and stumbled amid every kind of evil—he then sends out as his own vessels the souls of people who had withered amid every kind of evil, to oppose the one from whom he took them. Paul the persecutor was also a vessel of evil, an insolent man and an enemy of God; for he was fighting against God when he fought against [?]. “Whoever denies the Son,” he says, “also dishonors the Father.” Notice how the apostle himself disparages his former ignorance. “This saying is trustworthy,” he says, “that Jesus Christ came into the world to save sinners, of whom I myself am the foremost.” He takes the enemy of God, the zealot for the Law who unknowingly waged war against Christ, the vessel full of ignorance and zeal, and makes him a chosen vessel. And listen to him himself saying to Ananias, “Go, for he is a chosen vessel for me.” Do you see how he made a chosen vessel out of a vessel of evil? Elsewhere too Paul calls people vessels. “What if God wished,” he says, “to show his wrath and make his power known, and endured with great patience the vessels of wrath?” He calls the souls of unbelievers vessels of wrath. “To show the greatness of his mercy upon the vessels of mercy, whom he prepared beforehand”—us, the vessels of mercy. He says this of those who became worthy of his love for humanity and were chosen vessels. And this is precisely what is meant by “He ascended on high and took captivity captive.” He himself also points to the same thing. “When I am lifted up,” he says—that is, when I go up on the cross—“I will [?] everyone to myself.” Thus he brought to himself those who had been seized, and brought back the captives. He freed the exiles and healed the afflicted. He broke the bonds that sins had fastened, and in their place he put a crown on the heads of those who had been bound. And to learn that sins are bonds, listen to Scripture, which says, “Each person is bound in the snares of his own sins.” And because he found sins to be bonds, the Lamb of God, who took away the sins of the world, broke those sins. Oh, the love for humanity of the benefactor and Lord! When a master pursues a runaway slave and catches him, if he finds him free, he binds him; if healthy, he beats him; and if in the light, he shuts him away in a dark prison. But the Savior pursued human nature, which had fled from truth, from goodness, from the laws, and from the commandments. He found it not free but bound, and released it; naked, and clothed it. “All of you,” he says, “who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ.” He found everyone in prison and brought them out of prison; in darkness, and gave them light. “Land of Zebulun and Naphtali,” he says, “the way of the sea, beyond the Jordan: the people who sat in darkness saw a great light.”

And where did he find the prisoners and release them? In the error of worshiping many gods, as though in a pit and in an underground dungeon. And to learn that the pit is the worship of idols, listen to the prophet Jeremiah: “The heavens were astonished,” he says, “and the earth was horrified, for the people committed two evils. They abandoned me,” he says, “the fountain of living water, and dug leaky cisterns for themselves.” He calls himself a fountain because a fountain pours out water from its own springs, while a cistern holds water borrowed and brought in from elsewhere. For they abandoned the true God and strayed toward mere names. As Paul also says, “When you did not know God, you served those who were not gods by nature.” You lay bound in the pit of ignorance, in the dungeon of idolatry. Therefore David himself raises his cry of protest, saying, “Save me from those who go down into the pit.” Therefore blessed Isaiah also says, “The people who sat in darkness saw a great light.” And to explain precisely what darkness they were in, he adds, “The people who sat in darkness and the shadows of death.” The other prophet speaks directly to the giver of life: “By the blood of your covenant you released the prisoners from the waterless pit.” By “the blood of the covenant” he means the forgiveness of sins. And “prisoners”—as Paul was a prisoner of Jesus Christ, not from a waterless pit. And how was it by the blood of the covenant? It is precisely this: “This is my blood of the new covenant, poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins.”

And pay close attention. David says, “He went up on high and took captivity captive, and gave gifts to people.” All the prophets must speak in agreement, because one Spirit was in them all. This one says, “You released the prisoners from the waterless pit,” and the other, “Let them rejoice before you as one rejoices in the days of summer.” Let those who have been released, he says, rejoice as in summer. Therefore the Savior himself also said, “The harvest is plentiful, and the workers are few. Ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers out to work in his harvest.” In this way, he says, let those you have saved rejoice, like those who rejoice at harvest, gathering the fruits of their labor, or like those who divide the plunder. Powerful men take much plunder in war: gold, silver, and clothing. Everything taken is called plunder, because everything lies scattered and mixed together: clothing, weapons and swords, gold, silver, food, and whatever else there may be. In the same way, Satan had taken everyone and mixed them together. Christ came and snatched them all away from him together—the drunkards, the greedy, and the robbers. Therefore he says, “Let them rejoice before you as people rejoice in summer, and as those who divide the plunder.” As David also says, “I will rejoice in your words like someone who finds much plunder.”

See this marvel: just as when [?] wins a victory, binds the rebels, and rescues those whom the rebel has captured, the rebel always pictures death before his eyes, while the exiles rejoice because they have been released from tyranny and have entered the kingdom. Nevertheless, both the rebel who is to die and those who are to be freed are paraded on display because of the king’s victory. In the same way, the Giver of Life captured Satan and the demons in battle, along with those who had been captured by him, and parades them together on display. Paul speaks of both: “Christ,” he says, “is our peace, who made both one and broke down the dividing wall, the hostility, in his own flesh. He abolished the law of commandments with its ordinances, canceled and removed from our midst the written record that stood against us, and nailed it to the cross. He stripped the authorities and powers and openly exposed them to shame.” Just as people fasten a helmet, armor, or some other remnant of those killed to a pole as a sign of victory and carry it around, so he fastened Satan’s weapons to the royal standard and exposed the demons to shame on the cross. But the demons are humiliated and kept waiting. Indeed, those who had been carried off are also humiliated first and then go out into freedom. Listen to Paul: “Thanks,” he says, “be to God, who at all times leads us in triumph in Christ and spreads through us the fragrance of the knowledge of him.” The rebel is humiliated, and we who were under the rebel are also humiliated, so that it may be clear who won the victory, who the rebel was, and who was under the rebel. And because he captured the one and is going to kill him, but rescued and freed the others, these too must for a time be humiliated together with the one who is condemned to death and will go to his death. Isaiah speaks of such people who are to be humiliated and held captive: “The land of the Egyptians became labor [?], and the merchants of the Ethiopians and the Sabeans, men of great stature, shall come to you and follow behind you, bound in chains, and shall offer prayers to you.” To show that they come into captivity not for destruction but for relief, he says: “They shall follow behind you, bound in chains, and shall stand in prayer before you, because God is in you, and there is no God except in you.”

The demons are beaten, and the apostles are beaten: the former are struck with shame at their defeat, while the latter proclaim the king’s victory. The demons were beaten then, and the heretics are beaten now—those who, under the guise of members of the household, do the work of enemies. Just as war within a household is worse than any other war, so the error of heretics is worse than any other error. If a pagan insults Christ, I do not consider it strange, for he is an enemy of the cross. I say nothing against the Jew, for he is plainly an enemy. But the heretic who pretends to confess Christ yet denies Christ, who claims to preach the Holy Spirit yet blasphemes the Holy Spirit—his warfare troubles me like warfare within a household. Just as fighting within a city is worse than any other fighting, and turmoil within a home is more bitter than any fighting within a city, so the discord between husband and wife is worse than that within either the city or the home. Still more dreadful is the smoke that rises between the [?] and the [?], and still worse is the turmoil between the [?] and the stepchildren. Consider hostility within a household. [?] the man who comes home from the marketplace and faces a wintry storm [?]. When it is time for the meal and for rejoicing, he finds himself caught in warfare instead. Worries and sorrows multiply and make the harbors storm-tossed; at home he is amid the waves as though at sea. They leave the home and seek refuge in the marketplace as though in a harbor. God-fearing men endured such conflicts for Christ’s sake. Of them Christ said, ‘Brother will hand over brother to death, and a father his son, and children will rise against their parents. A son will be divided against his father, and a father against his son; a mother against her daughter, a mother-in-law against her daughter-in-law, and a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; and the master of the house’s enemies will be members of his own household.’ Just as warfare within the home is more dreadful than any other warfare, so the error of heretics is worse than any other error. They appear to share the same household ties and the same profession of devotion to God, clothing themselves in the outward appearance of godliness while fighting against the truth. Of them Paul says, ‘They have the outward appearance of truth, but have denied its power.’

And now, if we say the same thing, let no one be displeased by it. For the question is not whether we say only new things, but whether we can say something true, saying the same thing and explaining it in another way. Even though the message is one, its interpretations are manifold. God too is one, and he spoke in many portions and in many ways to our fathers, the prophets, and to the apostles. The fact that the same Holy Spirit spoke in both does not make us turn away from either the former or the latter; rather, we see one power and various workings. When the Father speaks in the prophets, the Son speaks; and when the Son speaks in the apostles, the Father speaks. When the Holy Spirit speaks in the prophets and in the apostles, the Father and the Son speak. There are no divisions there: the indivisible nature is not cut apart, nor is the undivided kingdom divided.

Do you wish to know how he is indivisible? Listen to the one who spoke to Moses when Moses was reluctant to go to the land of the Egyptians. “I am not able,” he says, “to enter Pharaoh’s house, for I have a weak voice and a slow tongue. I beg you, Lord, take someone else in hand.” When he saw that hesitation born of weakness was troubled by the command of the one giving it, he showed him who the craftsman was and who could fashion the bodily organ. He says, “Who gave a mouth to a human being? Or who made those who see and those who are blind? Was it not I, the Lord? I gave everyone a mouth, and I can give one to you. Having bestowed it on everyone, shall I deprive you, my prophet, of these gifts? Who gave a mouth to a human being? Was it not I, the Lord God?” And he says to Ezekiel, “Son of man, behold, I will raise up a horn for the whole house of Israel, and I will give you an open mouth.” He was not giving him the mouth he had from birth; rather, he calls boldness a mouth. Let us also seek this in the Gospel: who gives the mouth? “When they take you,” he says, “before courts, do not worry about what you will say, for I will give you a mouth and wisdom.” And it is clear that the one who said to Moses, “Who gave human beings a mouth?” also says to Ezekiel, “I will give you a mouth.” It is he himself who spoke in ancient times, worked in the prophets, and placed his power in the apostles.

Again, the Scriptures speak of lips—not visible lips, but boldness. When David says, “Lord, if you open my lips,” it is not that his lips were closed; rather, he asks for the boldness he lost. Otherwise, how could he even say those very words, “Lord, if you open my lips”? And in the Old Testament, before it was confused, there was one language among many languages. Moses wished to show that there was one speech and one language, and he says, “The whole earth was one lip.” Did all human beings have just one lip? Surely he called the single speech of their mouths “one lip.” “The whole earth,” he says, “was one lip and one voice.” And it is clear that everyone had one speech.

“I,” he says, “will give a mouth and wisdom.” And where do we find that he gave them? If we find that they were given to one person, then we will not doubt concerning the others either. “Some of the Cyrenians and Alexandrians arose,” it says, “and entered into questioning and dispute with Stephen.” Remember: “I will give a mouth and wisdom, and they will not be able to oppose you.” And they could not withstand the wisdom and the Spirit by which he spoke. See how God gives a mouth to the prophets, Christ opens the mouths of the apostles, and the Holy Spirit speaks in them.

But so that no one may suppose that the Son gives and the Spirit performs the action—as though giving belonged to one and acting to another—we must demonstrate that the Holy Spirit also gives. As it says in the Old Testament that he gives, so in the Gospel Christ says to the apostles, “I will give you a mouth.” We must ask: is the one who gives different from the one who brings? Even now, when kings give gifts, their attendants carry the gifts; they are not regarded as equals. Let us see whether perhaps the Son gives and the Spirit serves as an attendant. But so that you may learn that, just as the Son gives the word to the prophets and apostles, so the Spirit is not an attendant but gives abundantly, it says in the Acts of the Apostles: “When the Holy Spirit came and descended upon them, they spoke in various tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.” Paul says, “One and the same Spirit brings about all these things and distributes them to each individual just as he himself wills.” As he wills, and not as he receives orders. And again, to show that what he himself gives is also the gift of the Holy Spirit, and that what he himself brings about is also the activity of the Spirit, the Savior says to the apostles: “When they bring you before tribunals, do not worry about what you will say. For it is not you who will speak, but the Holy Spirit will teach you in that very hour what you should say.” Do you see that where the Father acts, there is the activity of the Son and the abundance of the Holy Spirit?

Where there is teaching and illumination and discourse about a way of life devoted to God, no created nature is found acting there, but only the uncreated nature. Whether in the illumination of baptism or in the ineffable mysteries, illuminating and sanctifying are not within an angel’s authority, but belong to the sovereign authority of the holy and uncreated nature. When he speaks through the prophets, it is not a created nature that speaks, but the uncreated [?], in accordance with the saying, “As he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets who have been from of old.” But when people are to be delivered from afflictions, God sends angels. Whether to deliver them from lions or to rescue them from fire, angels become servants of such deliverance. As Paul also says, “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent to serve those who are to inherit salvation?” But the Holy Spirit appears when the mysteries are to be performed, when the riches of teaching are to be bestowed, and when the ineffable mysteries of baptism are to be brought to completion.

And let no one be troubled in mind about receiving sanctification through water and the Spirit. For if, they say, the uncreated nature comes in the illumination of baptism, what need is there for water, which is created? And why, they say, did the Savior join the uncreated nature to the created nature? “Unless you are baptized,” he says, “with water and the Spirit, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.” And who does not know that water is created? But it is necessary to show plainly for what reason and for what purpose created water is joined to the uncreated Spirit. I beg you, do not grow weary of listening, and gather the meaning of these words into the storehouses of your minds, so that they do not flow uselessly past your ears. Just as water spread over the ground does not enter the earth or water the fields, but when it falls into a ditch and flows through the channels, it is not wasted over the ground but irrigates the fields, so now let my words not be scattered, but let their meaning irrigate the fields of your minds.

God gave many things to human beings, and he himself has no need of what he gave. But because our mortal nature is not capable of receiving invisible gifts, he uses visible things to accustom it to such things. The giver of life could have granted forgiveness of sins without water, and the manifestation of the Spirit would have been sufficient to wash the one who was bound, cleanse the filthy, purify the defiled, and bring the exile into adoption as a child. But because human nature longs for visible things and has only a small and very limited capacity to receive divine things with the eyes of the mind, he leads those who cannot rise so high and see invisible things toward them by an easier means. He set before them a visible example, so that through the clear assurance of their eyes their invisible souls might gain conviction.

Here is such an example. When God took the blessed Aaron, the brother of Moses, into his service as a priest, he said, “Clothe him in a flowered robe woven from threads of different colors, made of purple, scarlet, fine linen, and blue.” Blue, scarlet, and purple are familiar to everyone. As for fine linen, it is white like linen cloth. From these four materials of these colors they wove the precious robe, interweaving it with gold and precious stones. There was also a priestly turban for his head and a gold plate for his forehead, which bears the image of the Holy Spirit. On the priest’s belt were twelve precious stones: sardius, topaz, and emerald; carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper; jacinth, agate, and amethyst; chrysolite, beryl, and onyx. God commanded that all twelve stones be set in it: in the first row, sardius, topaz, and emerald; in the second, carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper; in the third, jacinth, agate, and amethyst; and in the fourth, chrysolite, beryl, and onyx. He commanded that the names of the tribes of Israel be engraved on the individual stones: on the first, the tribe of Reuben; on the second, the tribe of Simeon; on the third, the tribe of Levi; and likewise all the others, one by one.

He also commanded that the belt be put around the priest’s waist, and that the ephod, made of scarlet, fine linen, purple, and blue, cover his shoulders and be divided across his chest. “And you shall place,” he said, “two stones on the shoulders, one on the right and one on the left. On one you shall engrave the names of six tribes, and on the other those of the other six.” And why does he command that the names of the sons of Israel be engraved twice? Was it not enough to have them only on the shoulders, rather than also on the chest? He commands it twice because of their wavering minds. Again, he also says that there are to be pomegranate-shaped flowers at the collar of the robe. And thus he commanded the priest to enter the outer holy places.

And God commanded all this because of their ignorance, so that at least through such splendor they might regard the holy things with awe. But a priest’s honor is not purple, scarlet, fine linen, and blue, but righteousness, as David himself says: “Let your priests clothe themselves in righteousness.” But since the garment of righteousness is visible only to the eyes of the mind, and God’s purpose is not merely to increase the perfection of the perfect, but also to save everyone alike, when they see the great priest in divine splendor, they will reflect that he is the priest of the great God.

And to show that such a robe was made not because it was needed for the worship of God, but for splendor in the eyes of those who saw it, and that he has no need of it, but seeks sincerity of soul and delights in purity of heart—for this itself is royal purple and the flower of faith: having the virtues flourishing within oneself—he gave Moses this command: “When Aaron enters the Holy of Holies, let him take off the robe made of fine linen, scarlet, purple, and blue material, put on a linen robe, and enter the holy place.” Where God is to be seen, there is no need for outward appearances or elaborate robes. Even the robe that he himself ordered to be made for other purposes, he commanded him to take off. But so that he should not dishonor the holy place by the nakedness of his body, he commands him to wear a linen robe and linen shoes: simplicity and the absence of robes. This is why he seeks simplicity, for God delights in this, not in finery.

Nevertheless, brothers, although he gave Aaron the robe so that those who saw him would hold him in honor, he also planted there an image of things to come, so that nothing should be entirely without purpose, and so that he might enlighten the hearts of those who would come afterward. Blessed Aaron takes that robe and puts on the whole world at once, as though it were a tunic. For the world too is established from four elements: earth, fire, water, and air. From the earth comes the sweetest fine linen, from the peaceful earth; from the sea, purple; scarlet resembles fire, and blue resembles air, for the air often turns blue. But let anyone understand this however he wishes, provided that he does so with a mind devoted to God.

But let us consider the matter before us: why did he have the names engraved on the [?]? For the priest entered before the altar, while the people stood outside and did not dare approach. It was a cause of sorrow that only one person entered and enjoyed the holy place, while everyone else stood outside. God devises a means of consolation for their troubled minds through engraved gemstones. “You cannot enter on your own,” he says. “I will bring you in through the names engraved on the stones.” The priest entered bearing the twelve tribes and presented them all to God. The priest’s task is to present the people to God, for he is a mediator between God and human beings. He receives blessings from God and gives them, and he takes prayers from the people and presents them to God. It says, “The Lord said to Moses, ‘Go down and warn the people.’” See how he becomes a mediator from God to human beings and tells the people God’s commands. Again it says that Moses brought the people’s prayers up to God and brought God’s commands to the people. Therefore, when the prophet Malachi explained the priestly office, he said, “The lips of a priest proclaim knowledge, and they shall seek the law from his mouth, for he is an angel of the Lord Almighty.” He is called an angel, not because he has the nature of angels. Scripture calls the bearer of messages an angel; and angels are therefore called angels because they make God’s will known to the world. The name ‘angel’ is not a name for their nature but for their service. And because the name is shared, when Saul sent men to the prophet, it says, “He sent angels to tell him the king’s business.” Elsewhere it says, “David sent angels to Abigail, Nabal’s wife, to tell her David’s intentions.”

But what lies before us is to show that the priest was a mediator, and that he took up the people of God and bore the people's weakness. Whoever offers a sacrifice takes it to his breast and offers the sacrifice, for these are the distinctive representations of those who bring offerings. And whoever bears weakness bears it on his shoulders. For this reason he engraves the names of the people on the priest's shoulders, to teach the priest: “You who are strong must bear the weakness of the weak.” Paul also says this: “You who are strong, bear the weakness of the weak.” That priest was a figure of Christ. He took up, by their names, the twelve tribes of Israel—the entire people. But Christ bears still more in his body: the whole world. He also bears it on his breast, for he himself gave humanity rest upon his breast. And to understand that he also bears humanity on his shoulders, listen to the Lord's own parable. “Which of you,” he says, “has a hundred sheep, and, if one of them goes astray, will not leave the ninety-nine sheep in the mountains and go to seek the one that has strayed? If he finds it, truly I tell you, he will place it on his shoulders.” For this reason the Life-giver also carries the cross on his shoulders, because through it he bore the whole universe. “And Jesus went out,” it says, “and had the cross on his shoulders.” And why on his shoulders? So that Isaiah would not prove false when he said: “A child was born to us, and a son was given, whose authority is upon his shoulders.” The priest carries them in [?] and on his shoulders, for the priest's task is to present the people and bear the people's weakness. But let us return to what lies before us.

We mentioned that we would explain why water is joined with the Spirit. Just as there he gave the priest a robe decorated with various flowers—and God had no need of the varied colors of the flowers—so that he might delight the eyes of those who were under instruction, and they might be led through visible splendor toward invisible things, so also our God knew that the nature of the Spirit is uncreated, and joined the [?] nature to the uncreated nature, so that the eyes of the ignorant, looking into the water, might see the Holy Spirit as they see the sun in water. Do you not know that those who cannot look directly at the sun look into the water and see everything through [?]? You have not seen for yourself; at least look through the water. And from this very fact you find that the apostles were not baptized with water. But let them not quibble idly; rather, listen to the conclusion. For the apostles, since they were perfect and had received perfection before the cross of the Life-giver, were not baptized in water. Instead, the grace of the Holy Spirit was sufficient for them.

But the opponents immediately come forward against us. “They were baptized,” they say, “and the Savior bears witness. When he heard Peter say, ‘Not only my feet, but also my head,’ he said to him, ‘Someone who has washed has no need to wash.’ It is clear that he had received baptism.” They do not understand that he called the apostles’ baptism not water, but the word. “You,” he says, “are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you.” It is clear that by “washed” he means not baptized with water, but enlightened by the word, because before his sufferings he says, “Someone who has washed has no need to wash.” Yet after his sufferings, the cross, and the resurrection, when he was about to ascend, the disciples gathered together and asked him, “Lord, when will you restore the kingdom to Israel?” He said to them, “It is not for you to know the times or seasons that the Father has established by his own authority, but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you.” And what does he say after that? “John baptized with water,” he says, “but you will be baptized.” He did not say, “You have been baptized.” He said this after the resurrection, whereas he spoke of being “washed” before the resurrection. For if they had been baptized before his sufferings, he would not have said to those already enlightened, “You will be baptized in the Holy Spirit not many days from now.” And how was it “not many days from now”? Because he ascended when forty days after the resurrection were completed, and ten days later, when Pentecost was fulfilled, the Holy Spirit appeared. The Giver of Life said precisely the same thing: “You will be baptized not many days from now,” meaning after ten days. “You,” he says, “will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.” He did not say “in water,” but “in the Spirit,” because participation in the Spirit alone is sufficient to perfect and sanctify. “When the Holy Spirit came,” it says, “he arrived and filled the house where they were sitting.” There was no water anywhere there, so that he might make it clear that where divine power appears, there is no need for any action or material substance. Rather, the Spirit is sufficient to accomplish enlightenment even without water.

But God does not wish to dishonor the tradition of the mysteries on the pretext of perfection, lest you say, “Since I am capable of attaining it in my mind, what need is there for baptism with water?” Our intention in this has been to show that God can give the gifts of grace even without water. He is able to enlighten even without water, but we are not able to receive enlightenment without water. And since the Savior’s instruction took place for our teaching, we must bear in mind that even if we are perfect, no one is more perfect than Christ. The Giver of Life wished to remove every pretext, so that no excuse would be left to you for avoiding the water: first he himself was baptized in the Jordan River. But let us return to the matter before us.

When the Spirit comes to rest upon someone, he baptizes that person, even if the person has not yet been baptized in water. I do not mean only the apostles: in Cornelius’s house too, when Peter [?], while he was speaking, the Spirit came and rested upon Cornelius’s household. This was not done without purpose. The Holy Spirit knew that Peter’s conscience was troubled and that he hesitated to baptize them because they were Gentiles. For at that time the apostles thought that Christ’s gifts of grace had been given only to the Jewish people, and they recoiled and had scruples about giving baptism to those who were Gentiles. The divine Spirit wished to show that human minds cannot obstruct that gift, and he rested upon them before baptism, before they were instructed and enrolled. When Peter saw that the Spirit had descended and rested upon them, he said, “Can I withhold water from these people, who have already received the Holy Spirit, just as we did, without water?” Again, this same Peter explained the circumstances to the apostles who were in Jerusalem, for they took issue with him and said, “You ate and drank with Gentiles.” Peter set out his defense before them in order and said, “I was in the city of Joppa, and they summoned me there. While I was speaking the word to them, the Holy Spirit came and rested upon them, and I remembered the Lord’s word, which he spoke: ‘John baptized in water, but you were baptized in the Holy Spirit.’”

Do you see how water has been given for a certain necessary reassurance of human minds? For the person who is to be enlightened is himself twofold, [?] of body and soul. The soul’s nature is invisible, while the body’s structure is visible. God gave a twofold gift to these two parts: visible water for the visible body, and the invisible gift of the Holy Spirit for the person’s hidden soul. Royal gifts, likewise, are bestowed both by living hands and by lifeless implements, for the reed pen and ink are lifeless instruments, while the king’s hand is alive. Yet the king’s hand having need of the reed pen and ink does not make the reed pen and ink equal in honor to the king’s hand. Likewise, even if water is needed, like ink, so that the divine writing may be impressed through visible water, is water therefore equal in honor to the Spirit? Rather, we must understand that the Holy Spirit writes his act of generosity with water. Often written petitions were presented to kings. While the document is still in the hands of those presenting it, it is called a written petition; when the king puts his hand to it, it is called a deed of grant. Before the king adds his signature, it is a sheet of paper, still worth ten small coins. When the king puts his hand to it and confirms it, it is worth many weights of gold, and what was cheap becomes valuable. What used to sell for little sells for a great price. Although received freely, the gift reveals the extent of the generosity. Just as the paper, ink, and reed pen are of little value before the king puts his hand to the document, but once the king confirms it, you no longer look at the paper and reed pen, but at the gift bestowed by the king’s hand that wrote it, so also, when you see water by itself, [?] it is not worth even a single dang. But if you see that the Spirit has descended and rested upon the waters, understand that the invisible [?] is the master of sovereign authority through the Lord’s grace, and that what is visibly water is an instrument of invisible gifts of grace.

For this reason there is water—not so that it may be counted together with the Spirit, but so that it may lead you to the invisible. Where the nature of the one who calls people to himself is invisible, a visible mediator is needed, so that through the visible they may approach the invisible things. I will bring forward an ancient example. The laws proclaimed God, but he was invisible as God. He gave laws, so that they might not, through visible laws [?]; but he was invisible as God. He gave laws so that, through visible laws, they might learn the invisible things without despising them. Moses becomes a mediator between God and human beings, so that those who do not see God may look upon Moses’ face and through him see the invisible one. Moses is joined to God, not as someone equal in honor, but as a mortal who, through his face, serves as a guide to the immortal nature. They believed in God together with Moses, and in Moses, and in Moses together with God. But they were not to believe in Moses without God, for no one believed in a human being; nor were they to believe in God without Moses, for without a mediator mortal nature could not be led. For this reason the blessed Paul says that the laws were given, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. And Moses was the mediator between God and the people.

And see the remarkable thing. Scripture says, “The people believed in God and in Moses his servant.” Surely, because it said that the people believed in God and in Moses, Moses is not equal in honor to God? If Moses, though counted together with God, is not equal in honor to the Holy Spirit. Elsewhere Scripture says, “All the people feared God and Samuel.” Surely, because it said that they also feared Samuel, Samuel is not equal in honor to God? Rather, they feared the one as the Lord, and the other as a mediator. Likewise, when you hear of the mystery “of water and of the Spirit,” consider in your mind the divine riches of the Spirit [?], as true gifts, as uncreated grace, as an unending kingdom. When you see the water, recognize the mediation of the visible toward the invisible and divine nature, in accordance with the saying, “The people believed in Moses and in God,” and, “They feared the Lord and Samuel.” Elsewhere it says, “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon.” For Gideon was their commander and God their protector. It says, “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon”—of the one as king, and of the other as mediator.

I say all this so that you may not jumble your thoughts together aimlessly and fail to understand the various aspects of the meanings of words and things. Those who mix such words, names, and [?] together are like people mixing [?] materials together, as someone might mix gold, silver, iron, copper, and lead together. Likewise, someone whose thoughts are confused and who cannot distinguish things from one another is not acceptable, even if he offers a sacrifice. As God himself says, “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned; let his turning be toward you.” One must not only offer rightly but also divide rightly. What does dividing mean? To understand the authority of the Spirit and also recognize the mediating role of water. But if you mix everything together—Moses and God, Samuel and the Lord, water and the Holy Spirit—you will then find [?] materials mixed together. As God himself also says, “Son of man, the house of Israel has mixed copper, lead, and iron. Therefore say: Because they have mixed gold, silver, iron, and lead together, behold, I will receive you as smelting furnaces and melt you down to purity, so that you may no longer be mixed together.”

“But we do not find,” they say, “that the Holy Spirit is some divine power, but rather a gift of royal abundance. For it is written that the Holy Spirit is an anointing: ‘Jesus of Nazareth,’ it says, ‘whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit.’ Can the Spirit be God? Look, he is an anointing! And just as the character of the anointing is one thing and that of those anointed is another, so also,” they say, “the one who anointed has one essence, and the Spirit, who is the anointing, has another nature.”

And since the heretics seek only to reckon [?], without examining the meaning, merely pulling the words back and forth and corrupting the order of worship with human reasoning, let us too give them an answer: “Look, you yourself say that the anointing has one nature and those anointed another. You will also acknowledge that a fisherman has one nature and a fish another; a garment has one nature and a weaver another; shepherding has one nature and a sheep another; a laborer has one nature and a vineyard another. Will not their respective masters appear distinct from one another?”

Now pay attention. The Life-giver says to the apostles, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of people.” The apostles are fishers, and those caught in their catch are people. Now let the heretic say: “Just as fish have one nature and people another, so people must have one nature and the apostles who preach another. Just as the fisherman has one nature and the fish another, so those who learn have one nature and those who teach another.” Who would accept such deranged, disjointed words and not know that the teachers were from this world and the learners were human beings?

Moreover, the apostle says, “You are God’s building, God’s cultivated field.” Do you not know that a building has one nature and its builder another? And again: “Like a master builder, I laid a foundation.” If Paul was a master builder and they were a building, did the master builder and the building really have different natures? If you follow only the words, see how far the error spreads. Again the apostle says, “I planted, Apollos watered, but God made it grow.” And look, we see that those who plant have one role and those who water another; again, those who plant are one thing and the plant another. Does Paul, who planted, have one nature, and the Corinthians, who were planted by him, another? Why do you stumble over the words and not look at their meaning?

The Holy Spirit is called an anointing so that, through a name for something visible, he might proclaim invisible gifts. For in earlier times kings were anointed with oil from a holy horn, as were priests and prophets. But the Holy Spirit, who descended and rested upon the Life-giver as an example, and not because of any need, appeared without oil. And afterward he enlightened many without water and anointed many without oil.

And pay attention, I beg you: when the Holy Spirit wishes to display his works, he anoints even without oil. From where did Moses receive the ability to anoint Aaron, when he himself had not been anointed? Rather, because Moses was perfect, he received the resting of the Holy Spirit without oil. For the Spirit was in Moses, and for that reason he had no need of oil. Likewise, the apostles baptized with water and the Spirit, but they themselves were not baptized with water, but with the Spirit. Likewise Moses, who had not been anointed with oil but with the Spirit, anointed Aaron with holy oil.

He is called “Anointing” for many useful purposes. For the human race fell ill, and disease seized the whole world. He came and found the entire world paralyzed. He anoints it to heal its nature of [?]. He anoints it to train it for battle against Satan. What oil is to a competing athlete, the power of the Spirit is to those who contend against Satan. He calls the Spirit “Anointing” to show that he restored this diseased and mortal nature to immortal glory.

He is also called “Gift.” For the heretics say that the Spirit is a gift of God, since Scripture itself says that God gave the Holy Spirit to those who obey him. “The one who gives,” they say, “is one thing, and the gift is another.” If you call the Spirit a gift because he is given, then call the Son a gift as well, for the Son too was given. “God so loved the world,” it says, “that he gave his Son.” He gave the Spirit, and he gave the Son; therefore both are gifts. Can you deny that the Son is God because he was called the Father’s gift? Rather, he is a gift according to the divine plan, and God according to the dignity of his nature. The Holy Spirit likewise is God because of his authority, and a gift because of his intervention in the mystery. For whatever is given is a gift; yet that gift is often found to be a giver as well. God gave his only-begotten Son, and he was called a gift. Again, the gift too is a gift. “He ascended on high,” it says, “and took captivity captive, and gave gifts to human beings.” He gave and was given: he gave as God and was given as a human being. But let this suffice on this subject.

I know that I have prolonged this discourse, not to gratify any thought of my own, but to stir your longing. For you always long to see how the slander they cast upon the Holy Spirit may be exposed, because you are friends of the Father, beloved of the Son, and devoted to the Holy Spirit. Do not be surprised that I call servants friends: servants because of their nature, and friends because of grace. Listen to the Lord himself: “I will no longer call you servants,” he says, “but friends.” The Lord shrinks from calling them friends [?], and should we shrink? For this same reason Hananiah and his companions said, “Have mercy on us for the sake of Abraham your servant and Isaac your beloved.” And David said, “Your friends, O God, have become exceedingly precious to me.”

Let us say this boldly; let every mouth proclaim this same thing. For the mouths of the prophets have been entrusted to us, although we are not worthy of the prophets. The mouths of the apostles have been entrusted to us, although we do not come close to the apostles. Nevertheless, let us not cast away the honor entrusted to us, but sharpen our tongues—not to slaughter unbelievers, but to bring unbelief back and set it right. A bold mouth was the particular possession of the prophets. A bold mouth belonged to the apostles, who were firm pillars of the worship of God: mouths open and never closed. As Paul also says, “Our mouths are open to you, Corinthians.” Open mouths: “I will give you an open mouth,” he says. Our mouths too are open, for we are mouthpieces of right praise against heretical error. They are open and do not close. Even if our words fall silent, their effects do not cease. For God knows those who will be saved; he recognizes those who will turn back. Just because those who speak do not know into whom these words enter, does God also not recognize those who will be caught in the hunt?

The word of preaching is a net. Just as a fisherman spreads out his casting net and casts the net, the one who casts it knows that he has cast it, but he does not know what has been caught, because the instrument does its work unseen in the depths of the water. Likewise, when the casting net of the divine word is thrown into hidden souls, the one who speaks does not know who has fallen beneath the net. But God, who examines the net, knows which fish has been caught: which of those who fight against the Spirit the teaching of the Spirit’s divinity has brought beneath the net, and which of the Arians Christ’s glory has drawn in. God stands and examines minds and watches the workings of the casting net.

And to put another example to use: when they cast the net, its open ends stand separated and apart from one another, while it encloses the fish all around like a wall. There is a hollow of water in the middle, surrounded by the net. When they wish to draw it in, the open ends gradually approach one another until both sides of the net come together in one union, and end meets end. Likewise, in the first, far-off times, God appointed the prophets to cast the net, and in the second period, the apostles. The former cast the net with the old, and the latter with the new. From the two sides, the two companies of net-casters enclose a single hollow between them. The hollow in the middle is the east; opposite it are the west and the south, and facing it is the north. Listen to the verse itself: ‘They will come,’ it says, ‘from the east and from the west, from the north and from the sea, and will sit at table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.’

In that hollow, in that same enclosure, fishermen catch fish for destruction, but these catch them for salvation. Both sides come together, and the net-casters are found to have one nature and one craft, and the separated ends join one another. Likewise, at the end of this world, when the drawing in of the net is completed, the prophets will come forward and show their labors—how much they drew in—and these will show their own toil—how much they brought beneath the net.

The same net is cast even now, and it is not drawn by any hand of ours, but pulled by the apostolic right hand. If I say anything from my own thoughts, do not accept it unless Paul says it, unless Isaiah bears witness to it. The hand of the prophets casts it, and now the right hand of the apostles spreads out the net. But there is also another example to see. When the net is cast, the fish slips along and heads into its inner pocket. Often it also struggles and escapes altogether, as do the disciples of the heretics even now. See the wonders: at first Satan cast a net over the world, and the demons drew it in; but the righteous slipped away and escaped beyond the net, as David also says, “By my [?] I will pass over a wall.” Satan also spread his net in Babylon, to cast [?] over everyone. But the three holy fish leaped over the net with dry wings. And it is written that they said with the prophet, “Let sinners fall into his nets.” And because Satan cast an evil net into the world—he who said, “I have wandered and gone about beneath heaven, and here I am”—Christ came and wove [?] for him. Through the apostles he also cast nets for those whom Satan had caught, and brought the whole world under the net. What then? Are we inventing something from our own thoughts? Listen to the Lord himself: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, which gathers from every side.” May all of us fall into that net and be found among its catch. And this is the wonder: someone who falls into the net today as a fish catches other fish tomorrow as a fisherman. There, fish caught in the net go from life to death; here, those caught in the net are gathered from death into life. For this reason the giver of life says to Peter, “Cast your net on the right side,” and he gathered many fish. He teaches that through visible things we must come to understand invisible things. For he also says to this same man, “Do not be afraid, Peter; from now on you will catch people for life.” This means that you will secure them for eternal life.

May all of us henceforth fall into the net of right belief, dwell in the holy embrace of faith, and hold within ourselves the three patriarchs’ faith in the Trinity. For the heavenly Trinity is in heaven, and the three patriarchs are on earth. The nature of this one is not false, nor does the honor of that one lapse into denial. This trinity is divided in time and separated by place; but that one, timeless and eternal, always reigns, saves [?], and continually gives light. Through it may all of us be saved in Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever.
